mappings.note: Why the lesson only landed the second time, and what the Buddha did to change her, is about his method and her inner shift - the writer's message, LO-2.
Asks first what the learner understands by selfishness and then whether they agree with the text's verdict. An argued opinion, C-E1.2.
Splits a semicolon sentence into three simple sentences and compares the rhythm. Sentence structure and punctuation, C-E1.3.
'Sermon' is one of the words LO-7 names: settle its meaning, how it differs from a talk, and how it is used loosely. Dictionary-level word study, not context inference (LO-8).
Look up a box of words including 'procure' and 'lamentation' - the exact task LO-7 describes.
A pre-reading question drawing on general knowledge of the Sermon on the Mount. Conceptual understanding, C-E1.1; no word is being looked up, so not LO-7.
What she asked for and why she failed is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
The second errand for mustard seeds and its outcome are narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
His age at marriage is a stated figure; retrieval, LO-1.
The ten years of married life are stated; retrieval, LO-1.
The text glosses the Bodhi Tree as the tree of wisdom, so the answer is lifted rather than looked up; LO-1.
The subject of the first sermon is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
'Sakyamuni' is given in the text as his name; retrieval, LO-1.
A fill-in completing a line of the sermon. Extraction, LO-1; the questions that ask what the Buddha teaches are the LO-2 ones.
His age at schooling is a stated figure; retrieval, LO-1.
'Weary and hopeless' is the text's own wording; fill-in retrieval, LO-1.
What she asked at each house is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Completes a quoted line of the sermon; extraction, LO-1.
Completes another quoted line; extraction, LO-1.
Authorship of the lesson. Knowledge about the work, which no LO covers.
A discussion topic - seeing oneself as unique or as one among billions. The learner argues a position, C-E1.2.
A surviving fragment of a word-gloss exercise ('blessed - lucky'); its stored answer belongs to another item. Word meaning, C-E1.1.
What the flickering lights made her see - that death is common to all - is the moment of understanding the text is built around, LO-2.
The birth year is a stated figure; retrieval, LO-1.
The year of his death is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Medicine is what she asked for, as stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Asks what the Buddha's story means for the powerful - drawing out the writer's message and applying it, LO-2.
'What can be inferred about his method of teaching' is an inference about the Buddha as a character and teacher, LO-2.
What the Buddha says about the world is the doctrine at the heart of the sermon - the message, LO-2, rather than a single retrievable detail.
How Kisa Gotami came to see death as universal traces her change of mind, LO-2.
The four sights that drove him from the palace are narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
Where and when enlightenment came is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Identifies the comparison of human life to the city lights and explains why it is apt. Figurative comparison is a literary convention, C-E1.4, and no LO in this frame names it.
The death of her son and her search for medicine are narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
Benares as the chosen place, and why, is stated in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
The Buddha's purpose in setting the mustard-seed errand is his teaching method, LO-2, not a narrated fact.
What he did after enlightenment - begin to teach - is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
A 120-word speech draft with prescribed opening and closing lines. Structured composition, C-E1.2.
Relates an outside quotation to the Buddha's life and demands examples from the text - evidence-based answering, LO-3.
'Do you agree ... give a reasoned answer' about her selfishness. An argued opinion, C-E1.2, not a textual verdict.
